reference.source: Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: The most common inherited peripheral neuropathy, comprising many genetic subtypes with demyelinating, axonal, or intermediate physiology
CMT1 is a demyelinating form, most often CMT1A caused by a PMP22 gene duplication, whereas CMT2 forms are primarily axonal
Typical onset is in childhood or early adulthood with slowly progressive distal weakness and wasting, giving foot drop, high-arched feet (pes cavus), and hammer toes
Distal sensory loss, absent ankle reflexes, and 'inverted champagne bottle' leg contour from distal wasting are characteristic
Nerve conduction studies help separate demyelinating from axonal forms by markedly slowed versus relatively preserved conduction velocities with reduced amplitudes
X-linked CMT (CMTX1, connexin-32/GJB1) tends to affect males more severely and can show intermediate conduction values
Diagnosis integrates the clinical pattern, electrophysiology, family history, and targeted genetic testing, often starting with PMP22 dosage
Management is supportive with physiotherapy, ankle-foot orthoses, foot care and surgery, and avoidance of neurotoxic drugs that can worsen neuropathy
reference.pathophysiology: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease encompasses hereditary neuropathies in which mutations disrupt proteins essential to either the myelin sheath or the axon of peripheral nerves. In demyelinating subtypes such as CMT1A, PMP22 overexpression impairs Schwann cell myelination, causing slowed conduction and secondary axonal loss; in axonal subtypes the primary defect lies in axonal structure or transport. Because the pathology is length-dependent, the longest nerves to the feet and lower legs are affected first, producing the characteristic distal, symmetric motor and sensory deficits.
additionalDifferentials: Distal myopathies and spinal muscular atrophy variants
Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies
Friedreich ataxia and other neurodegenerative disorders with neuropathy
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to classify demyelinating versus axonal disease
PMP22 dosage analysis and gene panel testing
Detailed family history and examination of relatives
Foot and gait assessment for orthotic and surgical planning
Selective exclusion of acquired neuropathy causes when the picture is atypical
redFlags: Rapid or asymmetric progression suggesting an acquired inflammatory neuropathy such as CIDP
Prominent sensory ataxia or systemic features pointing to an alternative diagnosis
Respiratory or bulbar involvement, which is unusual and warrants reassessment
Sudden deterioration after exposure to a neurotoxic medication
reference.prognosis: Most forms progress slowly and do not shorten life expectancy, though they cause increasing distal disability, foot deformity, and reliance on orthoses; severity varies considerably by subtype, with some early-onset forms being more disabling.
pitfalls: Missing a treatable acquired neuropathy such as CIDP by assuming a hereditary cause
Prescribing potentially neurotoxic drugs without considering their effect on the neuropathy
Relying on gene sequencing while overlooking the need for PMP22 dosage analysis
Neglecting foot care and orthotic input that preserve mobility
management: There is no disease-modifying drug, so base management on physiotherapy and occupational therapy to maintain strength, flexibility and function
Prescribe ankle-foot orthoses and appropriate footwear for foot drop, and provide walking aids as gait deteriorates
Manage pes cavus, hammer toes and other deformities with podiatry and orthopaedic foot surgery such as tendon transfer, osteotomy or arthrodesis when disabling
Treat neuropathic pain and muscle cramps symptomatically and address fatigue
Avoid drugs recognised as neurotoxic, particularly vincristine, in patients with the disease
Monitor for complications including scoliosis, hip dysplasia and, in some subtypes, respiratory or vocal cord involvement
Offer genetic counselling and family assessment guided by the identified subtype and inheritance pattern
Coordinate multidisciplinary neuromuscular, orthopaedic, podiatric and rehabilitation care
